The Supreme Court recently pulled up the Maharashtra government for its poor performance in
implementing afforestation measures as compensation for cutting down trees while constructing
Mumbai Metro lines. Mumbai Metro Rail Corporation's measures, including tree transplantation,
were undertaken so ineffectively that it was obvious that compensatory and mitigation measures
are not high on the priority list while building critical infrastructure.


Developers are required to undertake compensatory afforestation when their projects involve
diversion of forest land or felling of trees. They are also required to implement measures to
mitigate the environmental impacts of their development. But there is a tendency to take a box-
ticking approach to such obligations. With climate and ecological risks rising, it is essential that
economic activities - like infra development projects - begin to take measures that hedge against
these risks. Understanding risks and the role that compensatory afforestation and environmental
mitigation play in reducing them will push developers to treat them as integral parts of project
design, rather than afterthoughts.


The top court pulling up Maharashtra government should serve as a wake-up call for
policymakers to systemically incorporate ecological and climate factors in their planning. Even
when infrastructure is considered green - as in the case of metro lines or RE transmission
networks - environmental impacts remain. Ensuring that these impacts are addressed is critical
for building resilient infrastructure. The apex court's rap on the state government's knuckles
should nudge both public and private developers, as well as policymakers, to review how they
understand and address climate and ecological risks.

This is something ’90s kids from smaller cities would remember: Lying on the terrace during
power cuts, staring at the night sky, counting stars, tracing constellations, and marvelling at that
hazy band of white light, the Milky Way. That view has vanished from Indian cities, even after a
cleansing evening rain. The culprit: Light pollution. As cities battle filthy rivers and toxic air,
with cloud seeding now the latest half-measure, few mention another pollutant — the constant
glow that is erasing the stars. We have flooded our nights with brightness so thoroughly that we
have forgotten what darkness feels like. There is something tragic about how our love of light
has become overexposure. What began as a victory over fear and darkness has turned into a
kind of planetary insomnia. The skies above cities never truly darken; they linger in a tired


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                    4


amber haze. Street- lights, billboards and glass towers spill photons skywards, bleaching the
heavens that once kept our time. Worse, we have learned to celebrate it. Satellite images of
glittering cities are passed around on social media as postcards of progress. India’s nighttime
glow has become a staple in growth story decks, every halo read as proof of prosperity. But
those glowing rings mark not success but waste, light meant for the streets lost to the sky.


The fallout runs deeper than aesthetics. Human biology ticks to the rhythm of light and dark, the
circadian cycle that keeps our sleep, hormones and metabolism in tune. Artificial light at night
knocks that balance off-kilter. A study in West Bengal found that city dwellers surrounded by
night-time radiance reported poorer sleep. Another, in Sleep and Vigilance, showed how light
pollution suppresses melatonin, the hormone that repairs cells and regulates rest. For other
species too, darkness is survival. Bats abandon feeding routes under harsh LED glare. Insects
spin around bulbs until they die of exhaustion. Each night, our lights erase a little more of the
planet’s nocturnal life. India has always revered light, though not this kind.


Progress should not be judged by how brightly our cities glow from space, but by how clearly we
can see the stars from our rooftops. Perhaps the first act of real advancement is as simple as
switching off an unnecessary light and looking up long enough to remember what we have lost.
If we can once again lie under a real night sky, trace Orion and find that faint, milky ribbon
above, we might rediscover not just the stars but something quietly illuminated within ourselves.

delivery options too, and he can feel damn macho by asking generals to tell him about America’s
5,000 nukes. So, what’s bugging him? Answer: Nuke geopolitics is crazy.

LEGAL REASONING


The evolution of international environmental law represents a fascinating journey from bilateral
treaties addressing narrow concerns to a complex web of multilateral agreements governing the
global commons. Prior to the twentieth century, environmental issues were primarily addressed
through property law or bilateral disputes concerning shared resources such as rivers or fisheries.
The industrial revolution, however, unleashed unprecedented environmental degradation that
transcended national boundaries, necessitating a coordinated international response.


The true genesis of modern international environmental law is often traced to the early 1970s,
when the international community began to recognize that environmental protection was not
merely a matter of domestic policy but a collective responsibility of all nations. This recognition
culminated in a landmark conference that produced a declaration containing twenty-six principles
aimed at inspiring and guiding the peoples of the world in the preservation and enhancement of
the human environment. The declaration articulated fundamental rights and responsibilities,
including the principle that states have the sovereign right to exploit their own resources pursuant
to their environmental policies, coupled with the responsibility to ensure that activities within their
jurisdiction do not cause damage to the environment of other states.


Two decades later, another historic conference was convened to address the accelerating
environmental challenges facing the planet, resulting in a comprehensive program of action for
sustainable development in the twenty-first century. This conference produced a declaration that

 built upon its predecessor while introducing new principles tailored to contemporary challenges.
 Among these was the formal articulation of principles that have since become cornerstones of
 international environmental jurisprudence, including the concept that where there are threats of
 serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for
 postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation. The conference also
 produced a non-binding statement of principles for the sustainable management of forests and

questions.stimulus:
The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties provides a framework for the invalidity,
 termination, and suspension of treaties, balancing the principle of pacta sunt servanda with the
 need for flexibility in exceptional circumstances. One ground for termination is supervening
 impossibility of performance under Article 61. This occurs when an object indispensable for the
 treaty's execution permanently disappears, such as the submergence of an island that was the sole
 subject of a territorial agreement.


 A much narrower ground is the fundamental change of circumstances, or rebus sic stantibus, found
 in Article 62. This is not a simple escape clause. It applies only when an unforeseen change
 radically transforms the extent of obligations still to be performed. The circumstances must have
 constituted an essential basis of consent, and the change must not result from a breach by the party


 12minutestoclat.com                                                                                   25


 invoking it. Boundary treaties are explicitly excluded from this rule, making it exceptionally
 difficult to prove.


 External events like the severance of diplomatic relations are addressed in Article 63. Such
 severance does not automatically terminate or suspend treaties between the parties, unless the
 existence of diplomatic relations is indispensable for the treaty's application. A more profound
 basis for termination arises under Article 64 concerning the emergence of a new jus cogens norm.
 If a new peremptory norm of general international law emerges, any existing treaty in conflict with
 it becomes void and terminates, ensuring the legal order can invalidate agreements that become
 fundamentally incompatible with its core values.


 The consequences of these events are outlined in Articles 69 and 70. For void treaties, such as
 those conflicting with jus cogens, acts performed in good faith before the invalidity are not
 rendered unlawful. For terminated treaties, parties are released from future obligations. However,
 any rights or legal situations created through the treaty's execution prior to its termination are
 preserved, maintaining legal stability. This framework ensures that while treaties are binding, their
 dissolution is possible in a controlled and orderly manner when confronted with truly fundamental
 changes.

The constitutional conflict between Parliament's power to amend the Constitution and the
 protection of fundamental rights reached a critical juncture in the landmark case of I.C. Golak Nath
 v. State of Punjab in 1967. The central question before the Supreme Court was whether Parliament
 could amend fundamental rights under Article 368, or whether such rights were immutable and
 beyond the reach of the amending process. The petitioners argued that fundamental rights,
 enshrined in Part III of the Constitution, were given a transcendental position and were not subject
 to abridgment or repeal by the amending procedure. They contended that an amendment under
 Article 368 was essentially a legislative process and would therefore be considered a law under
 Article 13, which prohibits the state from making any law that takes away or abridges fundamental
 rights.

 Article 368 was indeed a law within the meaning of Article 13. Consequently, if a constitutional
 amendment sought to abridge or take away any fundamental right, it would be declared void. This
 decision sent shockwaves through the political establishment, as it effectively placed fundamental
 rights outside the scope of the amendment process and threatened to invalidate previous
 amendments that had restricted property rights and other provisions. The judgment also introduced
 the doctrine of prospective overruling to ensure that its effects would not unsettle past
 amendments, but it nonetheless created a constitutional impasse.


 Parliament viewed this restriction as an impediment to its ability to implement socio-economic
 reforms through constitutional changes. The political climate demanded a response that would
 restore Parliament's authority to amend any part of the Constitution, including fundamental rights,
 while also clarifying the nature of the amending power. This constitutional deadlock set the stage
 for a direct confrontation between the legislative and judicial branches, ultimately leading to a
 significant constitutional amendment designed to explicitly overturn the effects of the Golak Nath
 ruling and reassert Parliament's supremacy in the amendment process.

questions.stimulus:
The transfer of ownership, or "property," in goods is a pivotal concept under the Sale of Goods
Act, 1930, as it dictates when the risk and title pass from seller to buyer. The Act provides a clear
framework in Sections 18 through 24, distinguishing between specific goods, unascertained goods,
and goods delivered on approval.


For specific or ascertained goods, which are identified at the time of the contract, the transfer of
ownership depends on the state of the goods and the completion of any necessary formalities.
Section 20 states that in an unconditional contract for specific goods in a deliverable state, property
passes to the buyer immediately upon contract formation. Crucially, this occurs irrespective of
whether payment or delivery is postponed. For instance, purchasing a specific car in a showroom
transfers ownership at the moment of signing, even if the vehicle is collected later. However,
Section 21 provides that if the seller must do something to the goods to put them into a deliverable
state—such as polishing or packaging—ownership does not pass until that act is completed and
the buyer is notified. Similarly, under Section 22, if specific goods are deliverable but need
weighing or measuring to ascertain the price, title remains with the seller until those acts are done
and the buyer has notice, such as with scrap metal sold by weight.


In contrast, ownership of unascertained or future goods cannot pass until the goods are ascertained,
as mandated by Section 18. Under Section 23, for goods sold by description, property passes when
goods of that description, in a deliverable state, are unconditionally appropriated to the contract
with the assent of both parties. Assent may be express or implied and can occur before or after
appropriation. For example, when a seller separates and marks specific bags of cement for a buyer,
the act of appropriation transfers ownership. Conversely, ownership may pass when a buyer selects
specific timber planks from a merchant’s stock with the seller’s silent assent.


12minutestoclat.com                                                                                 31


 Finally, Section 24 governs goods delivered on a "sale or return" basis. Here, ownership passes to
 the buyer when they signify approval, adopt the transaction (such as by reselling the goods), or
 retain the goods beyond the agreed time for return without rejection. These statutory provisions
 collectively ensure certainty in commercial transactions by pinpointing the exact moment
 ownership is transferred.

questions.stimulus:
Customary international law rests upon a dual-element foundation: State practice (the objective
 element) and opinio juris (the subjective element). State practice encompasses the tangible conduct
 of States, manifesting through diplomatic acts, legislative enactments, national court judgments,
 military manuals, and executive conduct. For such practice to generate customary law, it must
 meet qualitative requirements: it must be generally consistent (though not perfectly uniform),
 widespread and representative (including specially affected States), and may develop over either
 a lengthy or brief duration under the modern approach. A significant nuance concerns inaction,
 where silence or acquiescence may constitute practice, a principle illuminated by the Lotus case.


 The second element, opinio juris, distinguishes legal obligation from mere courtesy or political
 expediency. It requires that States believe the practice is legally compulsory. Evidence of this
 psychological element appears in government legal advisors' statements, treaty preambles, UN
 General Assembly resolutions, and diplomatic correspondence. The persistent objector doctrine
 provides a crucial paradox: a State that consistently objects during a custom's formation may
 exempt itself, thereby affirming the rule's binding force for others.


 Customary law assumes various forms and complexities. General custom binds all States
 universally, while special (regional/local) custom applies only to specific State groups, such as


 12minutestoclat.com                                                                                 34


 diplomatic asylum practice in Latin America. The relationship with treaties proves multifaceted:
 treaties may be declaratory of existing custom, serve to crystallize emerging custom, or generate
 rules that subsequently bind non-parties. The debate over "instant" custom questions whether
 norms can emerge rapidly from significant events without extensive practice.


 Participants in custom formation extend beyond States. International organizations contribute
 significantly, with UN General Assembly resolutions evidencing opinio juris. International courts,
 including the ICJ and ITLOS, influence development by identifying and articulating customary
 rules, while non-state actors increasingly shape normative expectations.


 At customary law's apex reside peremptory norms (jus cogens)—fundamental principles like
 genocide and torture prohibitions from which no derogation is permitted. These differ from
 ordinary custom through their non-derogable character. Relatedly, obligations erga omnes are
 owed to the international community as a whole. The orthodox inductive approach identifies
 custom by empirically examining practice and opinio juris, while the modern deductive critique
 observes that courts sometimes deduce rules from humanitarian logic rather than actual State
 practice, highlighting the persistent problem of proof in litigation.

questions.stimulus:
The Doctrine of Basic Structure represents one of the most significant judicial innovations in
 Indian constitutional law, emerging from the Supreme Court's effort to balance parliamentary
 sovereignty with constitutional supremacy. The constitutional crisis that necessitated this doctrine
 began with the conflict between Parliament's amendment power under Article 368 and the
 fundamental rights guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution. In the early years following
 independence, the Supreme Court had adopted a textual approach, holding in Shankari Prasad v.
 Union of India that Parliament possessed unfettered power to amend any constitutional provision,


 12minutestoclat.com                                                                              37


 including fundamental rights. This position was subsequently reaffirmed in Sajjan Singh v. State
 of Rajasthan. However, the political landscape shifted dramatically with the introduction of land
 reform legislations and the insertion of the Ninth Schedule by the First Amendment Act of 1951,
 which sought to place certain laws beyond judicial scrutiny.


 The conflict reached its zenith when Parliament enacted the Twenty-fourth and Twenty-fifth
 Amendment Acts in response to judicial decisions that threatened to limit its amendment power.
 It was against this backdrop that the thirteen-judge bench in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
 delivered its landmark judgment in 1973, propounding the Basic Structure Doctrine. By a narrow
 majority, the Court held that while Parliament possesses wide powers to amend the Constitution,
 this power could not be exercised to destroy or damage the essential features or the basic structure
 of the Constitution. The precise contours of this doctrine were left undefined, with different judges
 offering varying formulations of what constituted the basic structure. Some identified fundamental
 rights, judicial review, secularism, and federalism as core components, while others emphasized
 the balance between different constitutional provisions. The doctrine operates as an implied
 limitation on the amending power, recognizing that an amendment power cannot include the power
 to completely abrogate the instrument from which it derives its authority.


 Subsequent years witnessed the doctrine being tested repeatedly, particularly during the
 Emergency period when the Supreme Court in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain applied it to
 strike down portions of the Thirty-ninth Amendment. The doctrine was further refined in Minerva
 Mills v. Union of India, where the Court held that the limited amending power itself constitutes a
 basic feature, ensuring that Parliament cannot convert its constituent power into an instrument of
 constitutional destruction.

questions.stimulus:
Loneliness is no longer considered merely a personal misfortune; it is increasingly recognised as
 a public health emergency. Governments in the United Kingdom, Japan, and Australia have
 appointed ministers or commissioners specifically to address loneliness, a response historically
 reserved for infectious disease outbreaks. The impetus for this shift comes from a growing body
 of research. Chronic loneliness is associated with a 26% increased risk of premature mortality,
 effects comparable to smoking fifteen cigarettes a day. It raises the likelihood of heart disease,
 stroke, and dementia, while suppressing immune function and elevating levels of the stress
 hormone cortisol.Loneliness, however, is not synonymous with solitude. A person can live alone
 and feel deeply connected; another may be surrounded by people and feel profoundly isolated. The
 distinction matters because it points to the subjective nature of the condition: loneliness is a
 perceived gap between desired and actual social connection. This means structural interventions—
 building community centres, extending public transport to isolated rural areas, redesigning urban
 spaces to encourage incidental human contact—can reduce loneliness only if they also address the
 quality and meaning of social bonds, not merely their frequency.Critics of the public health
 framing argue that medicalising loneliness risks pathologising a normal human emotion and may
 divert resources from material poverty, housing insecurity, and employment precarity, which are


 12minutestoclat.com                                                                            44


 among its root causes. Others warn that state-led social connection programmes can feel coercive
 or hollow, especially for individuals whose isolation stems from grief, disability, or social anxiety.
 Support groups, befriending schemes, and community navigators have shown modest but
 consistent results in clinical trials, particularly when targeted at older adults and recent migrants.
 However, researchers caution that effect sizes are small, follow-up periods are short, and most
 studies lack adequate controls. Scaling what works in a pilot to an entire population remains an
 unsolved challenge. The broader consensus emerging from public health literature is that
 loneliness requires a multi-level response: one that combines individual support with the redesign
 of social infrastructure and a candid reckoning with the economic conditions that erode community
